messages.author: 5f8b51633aa2f2a1
messages.subject: Speeding Up ARMA Model
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to implement a general ARMA(p, q) based on the ARMA(1,1)
example in Section 7.4 of the manual.

My current code is below. It gets the right answer, but samples more
slowly than I'd expect. (I don't have any hard comparisons, just a gut
feeling)

Would vectorizing out the loops in the likelihood speed things up or
are those ok? Is there anything else I should check?

Michael

data {
int<lower=0> AR_ORDER; // Not using p,q b/c too easily confused with
multivariate series
int<lower=0> MA_ORDER;
int<lower=1> T; // Number of observations (length of series)
real X[T]; // Observed TS
}
parameters {
real c; // Constant Term (not TS mean!)
real AR[AR_ORDER]; // AR Coefficients
real MA[MA_ORDER]; // MA Coefficients
real<lower=0> sigma; // Shock SD (not TS SD!)
}
transformed parameters {
real mu;
// Mean of the time series (assuming first-order stationarity)
// X_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^p phi_i X_{t-i} + \sum_{j=1}^q theta_j
eps_{t-q} + eps_t
// E[X_t] = E[c + \sum_{i=1}^p phi_i X_{t-i} + \sum_{j=1}^q
theta_j eps_{t-q} + eps_t]
// = c + \sum_{i=1}^p phi_i E[X_{t-i}] + \sum_{j=1}^q
theta_j E[eps_{t-q}] + E[eps_t]
// mu = c + \sum_{i=1}^p phi_i mu + \sum_{j=1}^q theta_j 0 + 0
// ==> mu = c / 1 - sum_{i=1}^p phi_i
mu <- c / (1-sum(AR));
}
model {
// Priors
c ~ normal(0,10);
AR ~ normal(0,2);
MA ~ normal(0,2);
sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
// Likelihood
//
// Given a ARMA model of the form:
//
// X_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^p phi_i X_{t-i} + \sum_{j=1}^q theta_j
eps_{t-q} + eps_t
//
// At time t (conditioned on t-1 filtration), the only "random"
element is eps_t,
// which can be calculated as:
//
// eps_t = X_t - (c + \sum_{i=1}^p phi_i X_{t-i} + \sum_{j=1}^q
theta_j eps_{t-q})
// = X_t - M
//
// Then we have eps_t ~ N(0, sigma)
{
real err[T];
for(t in 1:T){
// Point prediction for X[t] all info available up to T (exclusive)
real M;
M <- c;

for(k in 1:AR_ORDER){
if(t - k > 0){
M <- M + AR[k] * X[t-k];
} else {
M <- M + AR[k] * mu;
}
}
for(k in 1:MA_ORDER){
if(t - k > 0){
M <- M + MA[k] * err[t-k];
} // else: M <- M + MA[k] * 0 so just skip
}
err[t] <- X[t] - M;
}
err ~ normal(0, sigma);
}
}

You can define M all in one go as:

M <- c + sum(AR[1:(t-1)] .* X[..whatever this needs to be...])
+ sum(AR[t:AR_ORDER] * mu
+ sum(MA[1:(t-1])] *. err[...ditto...]);

- Bob

Thanks. I've vectorized things ("arma2.stan", attached) [1] but the
resulting model is a bit slower than before, both for sampling and for
optimizing.

When I run the code, I'll see a few rejected samples: these are pretty
rare though--approximately 1 per 500 samples--so I don't think they're
the root cause (though I could be wrong).

Before I try to understand/eliminate those, is there any other low
hanging fruit?

Michael

observations, so hopefully not too big a deal.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding Up ARMA Model
parts:
Are you measuring with the same seeds?

I can't imagine a case where the vectorized form of
anything will be slower.

The only way I see to make it more efficient from
here would be to reduce the number of redundant
summations. There are many redundant sums here:

for (t in (1 + max(AR_ORDER, MA_ORDER)):T)

- c
- sum(AR_R .* X[(t-AR_ORDER):(t-1)])
+ sum(MA_R .* err[(t-MA_ORDER):(t-1)]));

Calculating a running average would be more efficient
(fewer terms in the expression graph, so faster derivatives).

- Bob
